title: Will they remember you?
principle: People buy the names that come to mind first.

screens.text: Let me tell you about a small dog. In the early 2000s, a phone company called Hutch made ads with a pug following a boy everywhere. The line was: "Wherever you go, our network follows." People loved that pug, and pug sales in India went up.

screens.prompt: In 2007, Vodafone bought Hutch and changed its name to Vodafone. What do you think it did with the pug?

options.label: Dropped it, to make a fresh start
Kept it, to carry people to the new name
Swapped it for a famous film star

screens.why: Vodafone kept the pug. In the new ad, the pug walked out of a pink kennel, Hutch's colour, into a red one, Vodafone's colour. The name changed, but the thing people remembered stayed.

screens.title: Mental availability
screens.text: Byron Sharp, a marketing professor, calls this mental availability: how easily your name comes to mind when it's time to buy. People pick from the names that come to mind. A shop they can't think of doesn't get picked, even if it's better.

screens.title: Things that remind them
screens.text: So what brings a name to mind? Things people link to you, even without your name: a colour, a sound, a character like the pug. Marketers call them distinctive brand assets. A funny line people repeat also carries your name.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: Phone networks are huge, but people forget small bakeries even faster. It's the first week of December. You pack every cake in a pink box. A mother who loved your cake in March just bought her son's birthday cake from a chain shop. She said, "I forgot your name."

screens.prompt: True or false: if your cake really is the best, families will remember you.

options.label: True: a great cake sells itself
False: they must also remember your name

screens.why: False. The mother loved your cake, but months later, your name didn't come to mind. When it's time to buy, people pick what they remember.

wrong.a: That's what most bakers believe. But the mother loved your cake and still bought elsewhere, because months later she couldn't remember your name. A great cake isn't enough.

screens.prompt: Which will help families remember your bakery months later?

options.label: A fresh new box design, a different one every month
The same ₹100 discount, posted every single week
Your pink box and ribbon, on every cake, always

screens.why: Yes. Seen again and again, the same pink box becomes yours, like the pug became Hutch's. Families think of you when they see it.

wrong.a: New designs look exciting, but families can't link any of them to you. Keep one look, the same pink box every time, so it becomes yours.
wrong.b: A discount brings a quick order, but people remember the deal, not you. Your pink box on every cake becomes something they link to you.

screens.prompt: Which WhatsApp status line will families repeat to their friends?

options.label: "Fresh cakes ready. Order now on WhatsApp."
"Best quality cakes at the best price."

screens.why: Exactly. It's short, funny and true to how people feel. You post it with your name and number every time, so when people repeat the line, your name travels with it.

wrong.b: It's clear, but every baker says it. Nobody repeats a line they've read a hundred times. A short, funny line gets passed on.
wrong.c: Every shop says "best quality, best price", so nobody notices it. A short, funny line is the one people pass on.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six things a baker might do. For each one, tell me: will it help families remember you?

items.text: The same pink box on every cake
A new logo every few months
Your name and number on a sticker on every box
A different name on WhatsApp and Instagram
The same funny line at the end of every post
Posting only when you have an offer

screens.why: Things that stay the same, seen often, help families remember you. Changing logos and names, or posting only for offers, leaves nothing to remember.

screens.setup: It's the first week of December. Christmas and New Year parties are coming. You have ₹10,000 to spend so families remember you. Each cake leaves you ₹450. About 500 families have bought from you this year.
screens.question: How do you spend it?

options.label: One big ad in the local paper for ₹10,000
options.outcome: Many people see the ad, once. Most forget it by the next day. 8 new orders come in December, leaving you ₹3,600. That's ₹6,400 less than the ad cost.
options.why: An ad seen once is soon forgotten. People need to see your name again and again, close to when they buy.
options.better: Give past buyers something they'll see every day, with your name and number.

options.label: A fancy new name and logo for the new year
options.outcome: The new name, logo and boxes cost ₹10,000. They look smart. But families who knew "the pink box baker" can't find you. Orders in December fall by 10. You lose ₹4,500, on top of the ₹10,000.
options.why: You threw away what families remembered. Even Vodafone kept the pug when it changed its name.
options.better: Give past buyers something they'll see every day, with your name and number.

options.label: Pink fridge magnets with your number, for 500 past buyers
options.outcome: Each magnet costs ₹20. You hand one out with every order and drop the rest on delivery rounds. When a party comes up, your number is on the fridge. 25 extra orders come in December, leaving you ₹11,250: more than you spent, and the magnets keep working.
options.why: Your colour and number sit where families look every day. When it's time to buy, you come to mind first.

screens.title: The honest line
screens.text: The line again: use on others only what you'd accept being used on you. Making your own name easy to remember is fair. Copying a famous shop's colours, so buyers think your cake is theirs, is a trick. You'd be angry if someone did it to you.
People buy the names that come to ___ first, so make yours easy to ___.
screens.why: Exactly. Vodafone kept the pug because people remembered it. Your pink box, your funny line and your magnet on the fridge do the same for you.

summary: Mental availability: when it's time to buy, people pick the name that comes to mind first.
Distinctive brand assets: keep one colour, one look, one funny line, and show them often.
A great product isn't enough if people forget your name. Never copy another brand's look.

cards.front: Your ghee is better than a famous brand, but it has no name people know. Who wins?
cards.back: People buy the names that come to mind first.

cards.front: What helps buyers remember your shop?
options: A new logo every few months
The same colour and look every time
cards.back: Distinctive brand assets: keep one look, and show it often.

cards.front: A big company buys yours and changes the name. What should it keep?
options: What people remember, like a mascot
cards.back: Vodafone kept Hutch's pug. Keep the thing people link to you.
